source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (matrix part)
finding: GPT-3 beat UCLA undergraduates on a text-only Raven-style matrix task, zero-shot, and showed human-like difficulty patterns.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40: GPT-3 above humans, odds ratio 1.88, p=.005, 95% CI 1.21-2.91. Item-difficulty correlation with humans r(30)=0.39, p=.027. Both found progression rules and more unique rules harder.
limits: Cannot exclude training-data leakage; text digits skip perception; GPT-3 era model.
agent_relevance: A base analogy skill exists in strong models, so O7 should elicit and check it, not teach it.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (letter strings and verbal)
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on letter-string and four-term verbal analogies, including SAT items.
numbers: Letter strings, humans N=57: GPT-3 better on zero-generalisation problems, OR 1.76, p=.0007; accuracy fell with number of generalisations in both. SAT analogy set of 374 problems: GPT-3 above estimated high-school-student average. Verbal analogy set also N=57 humans.
limits: Later work (Hodel and West; Lewis and Mitchell) shows letter-string success breaks on altered alphabets.
agent_relevance: A high score on a classic analogy item is not proof of general mapping.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (story analogies)
finding: On Gentner story analogies GPT-3 handled near analogies but humans clearly beat it on far ones; GPT-4 improved a lot.
numbers: Humans N=54 beat GPT-3 (OR 0.37, p=.0003); 15 of 54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3 reliable only in the near-analogy condition (binomial p=.0039). GPT-4 on 72 problems, via chat interface: near perfect on near analogies and more robust on far.
limits: GPT-4 tested only on story analogies, informally; run on 72 problems with context cleared between items.
agent_relevance: Far, relation-only analogy is where models are weakest. This is the case O7 most needs.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, GPT models drop sharply while humans stay level.
numbers: Mean accuracy over all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773] (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Humans flat across 0, 2, 5, 10, 20 letter permutations and symbols; GPT models drop at each step. Counterfactual comprehension check shows the models understand the new successor order.
limits: Models' score on the original problems was lower than Webb et al. reported. Only letter strings; prompt format matters (Hodel and West prompt used).
agent_relevance: Test an analogy on a changed surface form before trusting it. This is guardrail G3 applied to analogy.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Independent response to Webb et al: modified letter-string tasks make GPT-3 collapse while humans do not.
numbers: With a synthetic alphabet GPT-3 generative accuracy was under 0.1 on extend sequence, successor, predecessor and fix alphabetic sequence. Only remove-redundant-letter and sort stayed near the original range. Human accuracy stayed similar across modifications. In comprehension checks GPT-3 reached at least 30% of its original level on all but one check.
limits: GPT-3 only; small human sample; authors argue a problem set can be called zero-shot only if proven absent from training data.
agent_relevance: Do not read a model's score on a published analogy set as evidence of transfer.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Children and adults keep letter-string accuracy in Greek and symbol alphabets; every LLM tested drops with each domain shift.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin/Greek/Symbol: adults 0.88/0.91/0.89 (N=62); children 0.62/0.66/0.67 (N=41); GPT-4o 0.85/0.63/0.48; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79/0.74/0.27; Claude 3.5 0.68/0.62/0.46; Gemma-2 27B 0.60/0.39/0.14. Alphabet effect not significant for humans; p<.001 for each model after correction.
limits: Letter strings only; 2024 non-reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Frontier models of 2024 lose abstraction when the surface changes, so check transfer.

source: Stevenson et al. (2025) item-level results
finding: Item with a predecessor rule plus repetition was hardest for both children and LLMs, but LLMs could not use a rule they know when the alphabet changed.
numbers: Item 5 accuracy: adults 0.81, children 0.38, GPT-4o 0.39, Claude 3.5 0.20, Llama 405B 0.44. Item 1 (single successor): adults 0.97, GPT-4o 0.92. A Next-Previous Letter check was added to confirm models know successor and predecessor.
limits: Error types differ between humans and models; some human strategies not coded.
agent_relevance: Failure is in applying a known relation to a new domain, not in knowing the relation.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (main result)
finding: Analogical prompting: ask the model to recall relevant solved problems and knowledge before solving. It beats 0-shot CoT and hand-picked few-shot CoT on average.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% across GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM 2. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5 with this method 15% vs GPT-4 16%. Self-generating knowledge added gain over exemplars alone on Codeforces.
limits: Modest gains. Recalled examples are not checked, they may be wrong.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O7 (recall an analogous solved case).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) scale and K ablations
finding: The method needs a big enough model, and enough self-generated examples.
numbers: At text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001, few-shot CoT with labelled examples beat it; from text-davinci-002 up it won. Retrieval-based CoT better for small models, generation-based better for large. K=1 example underperforms; K>=3 helps (K=5 for GSM8K, K=3 otherwise).
limits: OpenAI and PaLM models of 2022-23 only.
agent_relevance: Use analogical recall only with strong models, and use 3 to 5 cases.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Self-generated irrelevant examples do as well as or better than relevant ones; correctness of the examples is what matters.
numbers: GPT-3.5, temperature 0. On GSM8K and MATH, random biology examples gave about 2.5% better average than self-generated relevant math examples; up to a 4% boost on GSM8K. Accuracy of the self-generated examples on MATH: relevant 62.0%, no-example variant 72.0%, random same-type 86.0%.
limits: Mainly GPT-3.5 (GPT-4o-mini in appendix); maths and BIG-Bench Hard only; not far scientific analogy.
agent_relevance: Weakens the cognitive claim behind O7. Check any recalled analogue by running it.

source: Qin et al. (2025) cheaper fixed-example variants
finding: Two proxy methods use one fixed set of correct examples for all queries instead of generating per query.
numbers: ICL-math and ICL-bio variants reached similar average performance, and both beat the original relevance-based method while cutting inference cost. Ensuring example accuracy gave better results on every problem type tested.
limits: Same limits as parent paper.
agent_relevance: Spend tokens on getting recalled cases right once, not on generating many per question.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Propose and solve analogous problems, then reuse their results to fix the first answer; plug-in on other prompting methods.
numbers: Reported average gains over baselines: +12% absolute in finding optimal solutions in shortest-path reasoning, +13% human preference in creative writing, +15% task completion in LLM-agent planning.
limits: Abstract and method read; synthetic or generative tasks; revision uses model-written analogue results.
agent_relevance: An analogy-then-revise loop. Fits O7 only when an outside check confirms the analogue's result.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives (zero-shot)
finding: Models spot near narrative analogies but fail far (cross-domain) ones zero-shot, below the 50% chance level.
numbers: 1,096 triples. Accuracy for (near,far), (near,near), (far,far), (far,near) partitions: GPT-4 94.0/92.5/57.1/29.1 avg 68.1; GPT-3.5 avg 60.3; SBERT avg 42.3; humans 98.6/97.2/96.8/91.4 avg 96.0. On far analogies models averaged 39.6% vs humans 94.1%. On near analogies models 75.0% vs humans 97.9%.
limits: Binary task; action overlap was the strongest distractor.
agent_relevance: Surface overlap pulls the model to the wrong analogue; make it state the abstract message first.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: few-shot and chain-of-thought
finding: Few-shot chain-of-thought (state each story's proverbial message, then compare) lifts far-analogy accuracy but hurts near ones.
numbers: Demonstrations of 2, 4 or 6 split between far and near. CoT helped more than plain demonstrations; on far analogies GPT-based models gained up to 30 points; on near analogies CoT still fell below zero-shot. Best model still about halfway between random and humans.
limits: Needs far examples in the demonstrations.
agent_relevance: Put an abstraction step (extract the relational message) before matching in O7.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: New tasks mapping words to letter or symbol sequences: advanced LLMs match humans in several conditions but react differently to semantic distractors and variations.
numbers: GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-405B matched human accuracy in categorical and dual-attribute conditions; in other conditions GPT-4 differs significantly from humans; older GPT-3 / 3.5 weaker. Human accuracy near 0.7 and 0.4 in two of the conditions quoted.
limits: Read abstract, methods and results text; exact per-condition figures should be rechecked before citing.
agent_relevance: Models give a how-possibly, not how-actually account of human analogy; judge by outputs, not claimed process.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Encoding Raven's matrices as language lets large models solve them zero-shot; higher-level abstraction helps.
numbers: On RAVEN Center, GPT-3 175B reached up to 77.2%, near human level; layout tasks 2x2Grid 87.8% and 3x3Grid 93.2% with decomposition, above humans. Ordinal naming beat random naming by over 20 points in larger models. OPT 125M accuracy doubled with an added abstraction.
limits: Matrices are synthetic and pre-parsed into symbols.
agent_relevance: Choosing the right representation before reasoning is a strong lever (O6, restate the problem).

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: On ConceptARC, GPT-4 text and vision solve far fewer abstract analogy tasks than humans.
numbers: Humans 91% overall; first-place Kaggle ARC program 52%; GPT-4 25%. GPT-4V visual one-shot 0.23 on 48 minimal tasks; text one-shot 0.25. Kaggle program 0.81 on minimal tasks.
limits: 2023 models; newer reasoning models score higher.
agent_relevance: Matches our own ARC finding that grid abstraction is hard for plain prompting.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a benchmark for long-text analogy evaluation
finding: Six-level taxonomy from word to metaphor; models find analogies harder to detect at higher levels.
numbers: Thirteen datasets (e.g. MSR 44,584 items; Google 19,544; others up to 100,000), eight LLMs, three distance measures; Mahalanobis distance best of the three. Performance falls as complexity goes up the taxonomy.
limits: Embedding-distance method, not generative prompting; per-model numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Plain embedding similarity cannot find deep analogues; do not use cosine retrieval as the analogy engine.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models
finding: InstructGPT can generate analogies; the best prompts are precise imperatives at low temperature.
numbers: Human evaluation of 1,407 analogies, 3 raters each. Largest InstructGPT reached human-level quality when asked for an analogous concept (no source given) and fell below human quality when asked to explain a given source-target pair. Quality rose with model size (0.3B to 1.3B: 19.17% and 15.34% relative gains in two settings). Spelling errors cut scores 3 to 7% relative.
limits: Automatic metric BLEURT could not judge soundness; human check was needed.
agent_relevance: Use low temperature and imperative wording for analogy slots. Do not judge analogy quality by text overlap.

source: Stevenson, Smal, Baas, Grasman, van der Maas (2022) Putting GPT-3's creativity to the (Alternative Uses) test
finding: Humans scored higher on originality and surprise; GPT-3 scored higher on usefulness in the Alternative Uses Task.
numbers: 42 humans vs 144 GPT-3 runs (781 GPT responses analysed). Humans higher originality (beta .17, p=.004) and surprise (beta .14, p<.05); GPT-3 higher utility (beta .10, p<.001). Originality and utility negatively correlated in both groups (r=-.56 humans, -.61 GPT-3). Humans more flexible (F(1,85)=5.53, p=.021). Inter-rater ICC .57 originality, .68 utility, .67 surprise.
limits: GPT-3 only; 2022; flexibility not tied to temperature (r=.04).
agent_relevance: Originality and usefulness trade off; selection must test both, and code can test usefulness.

source: Franceschelli and Musolesi (2025) On the creativity of large language models
finding: Review applying Boden's three creativity types (combinational, exploratory, transformational) to LLMs.
numbers: No new experiment numbers. Argues current LLMs fit combinational and exploratory creativity best, and training on past text limits transformational novelty.
limits: Position paper; only the framing was used.
agent_relevance: Use LLMs for recombination and exploration (O7), keep the novelty test outside the generator.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning (diversity)
finding: Plain and cross-domain prompting mode-collapse; an analogy-first pipeline (AR) raises diversity sharply.
numbers: 50 research problems, 150 generations each; Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash at temperature 1. Baselines: domain Vendi 2.64 (no-domain) and 2.84 (cross-domain); solution Vendi 5.81 and 8.34; only about 5% of domains and 57-66% of solutions unique. AR raised domain Vendi 100-115% and solution Vendi 90-173%.
limits: Preprint (May 2026); AR uses extra LLM calls; the cross-domain baseline without explicit analogies stayed collapsed.
agent_relevance: Best fit for O7: generate analogies to distant domains first, then search for solutions through them.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) AR: novelty and biomedical tests
finding: AR solutions were more often novel by LLM judge and by human pairwise vote, and worked on four biomedical tasks.
numbers: Binary novelty, no-domain / cross-domain / AR: Claude 1.6% / 21.6% / 50.4%; GPT 8.8% / 27.2% / 58.8%; Gemini 8.6% / 37.9% / 68.8%. Humans picked AR as more novel in 78% of pairs (kappa .445) against cross-domain. Perturbation prediction about 13-fold gain on a distributional metric; brain-region links Spearman .729; state of the art on 2 oligonucleotide datasets.
limits: Novelty judged by an LLM against literature; our G8 says model novelty judges are weak, so treat as an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Evidence that explicit analogy beats 'think of other fields' prompting, with some real downstream tests.

source: Guo (2025) LacMaterial: LLMs as analogical chemists for materials discovery
finding: LLM prompted with cross-domain analogies (airport, postal system) to propose battery electrolyte candidates beyond usual dopant substitutions.
numbers: Case study on LLZO electrolyte and NMC811 cathode with candidate tables and an ablation of the lead candidate; no wet-lab or large-sample test reported.
limits: Evidence is anecdotal; computational plausibility only.
agent_relevance: Shows how an O7 prompt can be phrased: abstract the rule, give a retrieval case, then map. Needs outside validation.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SciMON: Scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty
finding: Retrieves inspirations from past papers (semantic, citation and knowledge-graph neighbours) and rewrites ideas until novel versus prior work.
numbers: Human study I: GPT-4 few-shot ranked above zero-shot in 65% of cases. Iterative novelty boosting: first-iteration ideas gained novelty in 54.4% (GPT4FS), 55.6% (+SN); second iteration +57.8%; about 22 new terms per iteration. GPT4FS+KG judged more technically detailed in 48% of pairs and less incremental in 45%. GPT-4 ideas overall low in technical depth and novelty versus real papers.
limits: Six NLP-expert raters, 50 items in study I; NLP papers only; novelty measured against retrieved papers.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of cross-literature inspiration plus a novelty-check loop implements O7/O6. The check uses retrieval, not model opinion (fits G8).

source: Li et al. (2022) Mind's Eye: grounded language model reasoning through simulation
finding: A physics engine (MuJoCo) runs the scenario and its result is fed to the LM; a code-run mental model.
numbers: UTOPIA benchmark, 39 tasks. Absolute accuracy gain 27.9% zero-shot and 46.0% few-shot on average. Vanilla GPT-3 175B: 24% zero-shot, 38.2% few-shot. Few-shot in one comparison: 36.4 to 38.2% with plain LM vs 46.7 to 84.2% with Mind's Eye. GPT-3 1.3B plus Mind's Eye 29.8% vs vanilla 175B 29% (100x smaller). Conversion error cost 3.6 to 4.7 points.
limits: 2022 models; physics tasks that map to a simulator; needs a text-to-simulation converter.
agent_relevance: Closest working form of Nersessian's simulative mental model inside an LLM: run it, trust the output (G2, G3).

source: Eisape et al. (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: Johnson-Laird style syllogisms: larger PaLM 2 models beat humans on logic yet share human biases (variable order, fallacies).
numbers: Within the PaLM 2 family larger models are more logical and more accurate than humans; the best model only about 75% on some sets; models give confident wrong answers on syllogistic fallacies; accuracy of all models 0% by design on a no-valid-conclusion probe.
limits: PaLM 2 only; first pages and method read.
agent_relevance: Mental-model-style errors are copied by LLMs. Shuffle premise order and compare answers.
